title: State v. Priya Raman
summary: A late-night bar fight left the complainant with a broken nose. The accused says she acted in self-defence. Messages sent after the incident raise a witness-interference concern.
jurisdictionNote: Training case set in a fictional common-law jurisdiction. Names, events and rules are invented for instruction and are not legal advice.

defendant.name: Priya Raman
defendant.background: Registered nurse with no previous convictions. Lives alone in a rented flat near the hospital where she works.

facts.text: At about 23:40 at the Copper Lantern bar, Raman punched Daniel Voss once in the face, breaking his nose.
Bar CCTV shows Voss shoving Raman backwards into a table about five seconds before the punch. It does not show what was said.
The next morning Raman sent Voss three text messages, including: "You'll regret it if you keep talking to the police about me."
Police arrested Raman at the bar. Before any caution was given, an officer asked her: "What happened here?" She replied: "He grabbed me first, so I hit him. He deserved it."
Voss's friend, Ella Brandt, is the only eyewitness besides the two of them. She is due to give evidence for the prosecution.

At trial the jury rejected self-defence and convicted. Raman has no previous convictions and has written a letter of apology. Her employer says a custodial sentence would end her nursing registration.

exhibits.title: Accused's statement at the scene
exhibits.description: Officer's notebook entry recording Raman's words: "He grabbed me first, so I hit him. He deserved it."
exhibits.provenance: Recorded by the arresting officer about two minutes after arrest, in reply to the question "What happened here?" No caution had been given. The caution was first given at the police station forty minutes later.
exhibits.objection: The defence says the statement was obtained by questioning an arrested person before any caution, in breach of the questioning rules, and must be excluded.

decisionPoints.title: Bail application
decisionPoints.prompt: Raman applies for bail pending trial. The prosecution opposes unconditional release because of the messages sent to the complainant.

submissions.prosecution: The messages are a thinly veiled threat to a complainant who is cooperating with police, and the only independent eyewitness is his friend. We seek a no-contact condition, a ban on attending the bar, and residence at her address.
submissions.defence: She is a nurse of good character with no record, and the messages were sent in anger the morning after. She should be released without conditions.

factors.text: Text messages to the complainant the morning after, including "You'll regret it if you keep talking to the police about me."
The complainant and the only independent eyewitness are both due to give evidence.
No previous convictions; a stable job and address.
Conditions may be imposed whenever they are necessary to manage a real risk, such as interference with witnesses, whatever the accused's record.

options.label: Release without conditions
options.feedback: This ignores a direct, threatening contact with the complainant about his evidence. The interference risk is real and needs managing.

options.label: Release with no-contact, exclusion and residence conditions
options.feedback: Her good character supports release, and the specific interference risk created by the messages is fully addressed by a no-contact condition and exclusion from the bar.

options.label: Refuse bail and remand in custody
options.feedback: The interference concern is genuine, but for someone of good character conditions can manage it, so custody goes further than necessary.

advice.rationale: I would release Ms Raman on conditions. Her good character and stable life support release, but her message warning Mr Voss that he would regret talking to the police is a real risk of witness interference. A no-contact condition covering him and Ms Brandt, exclusion from the bar and a residence condition manage that risk without custody.

I would release Ms Raman without conditions. She has no previous convictions, a stable job and a fixed address, and this was a single incident on a night out. There is nothing to suggest she will abscond or reoffend, so conditions would be unnecessary.
advice.flawExplanation: The advice ignores the messages to the complainant (F3), which create the very risk that justifies conditions: interference with prosecution witnesses.

advice.rationale: I would release Ms Raman without conditions. With no previous convictions she is entitled to unconditional bail, and conditions are reserved for accused people whose record shows they cannot be trusted. Her messages can be raised at trial.
advice.flawExplanation: Conditions do not depend on a criminal record. They may be imposed whenever necessary to manage a real risk, including interference with witnesses.

decisionPoints.title: Admissibility of the statement at the scene
decisionPoints.prompt: The prosecution tenders exhibit P-2, Raman's words to the arresting officer. The defence applies to exclude it.

submissions.prosecution: It was a brief, natural exchange at the scene, not an interview. The statement is reliable and highly relevant to the rejected self-defence claim.
submissions.defence: She had been arrested. The officer asked her a direct question about the offence without cautioning her. That is exactly what the caution rule exists to prevent.

factors.text: Raman had already been arrested when the question was asked.
Her words were a reply to the officer's question "What happened here?", not a spontaneous remark.
No caution was given until the police station, forty minutes later.
A person under arrest must be cautioned before being questioned about the offence. Answers obtained in breach are excluded unless admitting them would not undermine the fairness of the trial.
"He deserved it" is significant evidence against self-defence.

options.label: Admit the statement
options.feedback: The statement was a reply to questioning about the offence after arrest and before caution. Its importance to the prosecution makes the unfairness worse, not better.

options.label: Admit with a direction about the missing caution
options.feedback: A jury direction cannot cure a breach that goes to the heart of the right not to incriminate oneself. The statement should not go before the jury at all.

options.label: Exclude the statement
options.feedback: This was questioning about the offence after arrest without a caution, and the answer is damaging on the central issue. Admitting it would undermine the fairness of the trial.

advice.rationale: I would exclude the statement. Ms Raman had been arrested, and the officer asked her directly what happened, so this was questioning about the offence without a caution. Because her answer goes to the central issue of self-defence, admitting it would undermine the fairness of the trial.

I would admit the statement. Ms Raman volunteered it spontaneously as officers arrived, before anyone had asked her a question, and the caution rule does not cover unprompted remarks. It is also highly relevant to self-defence.
advice.flawExplanation: The record says she was answering the officer's question "What happened here?" after arrest (F4). It was not volunteered. The advice's whole analysis rests on that misreading.

advice.rationale: I would admit the statement. The caution requirement applies to formal interviews at the police station, and a quick question at the scene is not an interview. Its relevance to self-defence makes it important for the jury to hear.
advice.flawExplanation: The caution rule applies to any questioning of an arrested person about the offence, wherever it happens. It is not limited to formal station interviews.

decisionPoints.title: Sentence
decisionPoints.prompt: The jury convicted Raman of assault occasioning actual bodily harm. The sentencing range runs from a community order to two years' custody.

submissions.prosecution: A punch to the face causing a fracture. She also sent threatening messages afterwards, and she showed no remorse at trial.
submissions.defence: One punch, provoked by a shove into a table. She is of previous good character, has apologised in writing, and would lose her career if sent to custody.

factors.text: A single punch, causing a broken nose.
CCTV shows the complainant shoved her into a table seconds before.
A written apology after the verdict.
Custody would end her nursing registration.
She pleaded not guilty and contested the case at trial.
Threatening messages sent to the complainant the next morning.

options.label: Community order with compensation to the complainant
options.feedback: A single provoked blow by a woman of good character, with an apology, sits below the custody threshold. The messages aggravate the offence, but not enough to require custody.

options.label: Short custodial sentence
options.feedback: The fracture and the messages make custody arguable, but provocation, good character and the apology weigh against it.

options.label: Custody toward the top of the range
options.feedback: The upper range is for sustained or weapon-assisted assaults. Nothing here comes close to that.

advice.rationale: I would impose a community order with compensation. A single punch that broke Mr Voss's nose is serious, and her messages afterwards aggravate it, but the CCTV shows she was shoved into a table moments before. With her good character and written apology, this falls below the custody threshold.

I would sentence toward the top of the range. Ms Raman put the complainant through a trial instead of accepting responsibility, and her decision to contest the case shows a lack of remorse that aggravates the offence. A substantial custodial term is needed.
advice.flawExplanation: Pleading not guilty is not an aggravating factor. A contested trial only means she gets no credit for a guilty plea, and it cannot be used to increase the sentence.

advice.rationale: I would impose a short custodial sentence. She deliberately struck the complainant in the face, causing a fracture, and then sent him threatening messages. Her good character and apology reduce the term but do not avoid custody.
advice.flawExplanation: The advice leaves out the provocation shown on CCTV, the shove into a table seconds before the punch (F2), which substantially reduces her culpability.
